name: PT Sreeya Sewu Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sreeya Sewu Indonesia: a feed integrator priced for a margin it has never earned
frontmatter.summary: Sreeya Sewu trades a long way above the value its own earning power supports. The audited depreciation charge is several times the data-pack figure, a quarter of the rebuilt EBITDA is a fair-value credit, and even on that corrected base the shares capitalise a margin no year in the record has produced. Nine-month 2026 moved to a loss as corn and soybean meal rose while the scaled peers grew. Our target is a discounted book-value floor. SELL.
thesis: The data pack understates depreciation; restating it from the audited notes lifts EBITDA, but the fair-value credit inside that EBITDA has to come out, and at the market price the enterprise is still capitalised at a multiple a thin-margin integrator cannot earn.

The nine-month 2026 loss is witnessed evidence rather than forecast; feed cost is mostly raw material, corn and soybean meal rose sharply, pass-through is only partial, and the peer leaders earned double-digit operating margins in the same nine months.
Return on operating capital sits in the low single digits against a double-digit cost of capital, so growth in this configuration destroys value and we do not pay for the expansion plan.
Both earnings-based valuation methods return no equity value once September net debt is deducted; the target rests on book value, further discounted because the shares are barely tradeable.

The float is the exit problem. Public shareholders hold well below the exchange minimum and the cheapest route to compliance for the controller is a tender or a block, not a recovery in the milling margin.

catalysts.event: Year-end corn harvest and the domestic corn basis into the first quarter
The national feed-corn allocation for the coming crop year and any revision to the corn reference price
Audited FY2026 results and the FY2027 raw-material cost base
AGM vote on the dividend and on any capital action to lift the public float

blocks.text: We initiate **Sreeya Sewu Indonesia (SIPD)** at **SELL** with a target of **Rp189** against a last price of **Rp630**, a total return of **-70.0%**. The gap is not a disagreement about the cycle. It is a disagreement about what the asset is worth at all.

Three facts carry the call. The first is arithmetic. The data pack that every screen in the market carries shows a depreciation and amortisation charge of a fraction of the real one, because IDX issuers file cash-flow statements on the direct method and the pack's model reads the difference as a running cost rather than a non-cash charge. Taken from the audited segment note, the charge is 98.2 and the rebuilt EBITDA is 183.5 on sales of 5,441.5 [S3]. On that corrected base the shares trade at 9.0x of last year's EBITDA and 26.9x of the year we expect to be the trough. Neither multiple is a bargain for a processor whose gross margin is a single digit and whose return on operating capital is a fraction of its cost of capital.

The second is that the rebuilt figure is not all earnings. A fair-value credit on biological assets of 49.1 IDR bn sits inside the 183.5 [S3], and a further 9.2 IDR bn sits inside the nine-month 2026 result [S4]. It is a mark-to-model on live birds and hatching eggs, priced off projected selling prices and feed costs [S4]. Strip it out and the multiple on clean EBITDA is roughly a third higher than the screen shows. We quote the reported restated figure for comparability — that is what the market's own numbers will converge on — but a valuation that leans on a mark-to-model credit is leaning on the live-bird price, and the live-bird price is falling.

The third is the income statement itself. In the first nine months of 2026 the company sold 4,301 IDR bn and lost 59.2 IDR bn [S4]. That is not a modelling artefact; it is the witnessed consequence of a cost base in which raw materials are the overwhelming majority of cost of sales [S5], exposed to corn and soybean meal that rose hard through the year. The house agricultural deck still carries corn at US$215/t and soybean meal at US$411/t for the year, above the prior year's average, so the pressure is with us rather than behind us. And it is not the sector: over the same nine months CPIN earned 5.2 IDR tn of net profit on an operating margin of 11.3% and JPFA 3.2 IDR tn, both up double digits on the year [S9]. A cyclical trough that the scaled integrators are already climbing out of does not explain SIPD's loss.

Our valuation says something uncomfortable and simple: the operating assets earn less than they cost, so they are worth less than the capital sunk into them. The DCF values the enterprise at 405.5, which does not cover the debt of 982 IDR bn less the cash of 117 IDR bn on the September balance sheet [S4]. Unfloored, that is a negative equity value of roughly a quarter of the share price per share. The peer-median EV/EBITDA cross-check, run on last year's restated EBITDA rather than on the trough, also leaves nothing for shareholders. Only book value survives, and we hold book value at the peer median of 1.0 — a multiple that assumes the assets are worth what the balance sheet says even though they currently earn nothing on them.

The arithmetic runs one way. The weighted method blend is Rp185 — the two earnings methods return exactly zero, so it is the book leg times its 30% weight; rolled forward at the cost of equity it is Rp214; probability-weighted across our scenarios it is Rp270, because the bull case alone carries the lift; after the single liquidity haircut it is Rp189.

Three things move the value, and we watch all three. The raw-material spread comes first: corn and soybean meal set the cost line and the live-bird and dressed-chicken prices set what can be passed on. The second is utilisation: dressed-chicken capacity was built ahead of demand and runs at roughly 50.0% per cent [S5], so every extra tonne carries almost no incremental fixed cost — or, in the other direction, leaves the fixed base stranded. The third is the balance sheet: net debt has risen through the quarters we can see, interest absorbs a large part of operating profit, and the company pays no dividend to fall back on [S5].

What would change our mind is not a better price. It is evidence that the margin can be lifted structurally — a sustained fall in the corn basis, a DOC price that restores breeder economics, or a capital structure that stops the interest line from eating the recovery. None of those is in the filings today.

A poultry integrator in this market buys energy and protein, converts them into feed, converts feed
into birds, and sells the bird or the cut. The value added is thin because the product is a
commodity: buyers can switch supplier on price, and the farmer's willingness to pay is capped by what
the live bird fetches at the farm gate. Feed millers therefore live on the spread between the cost of
the ration and the price of the ration, and on how much of a raw-material move they can pass through
before the customer walks. When the farm-gate price falls below the farmer's own cost, the first thing
that breaks is the order book for chicks and feed, which is why an integrator with a breeder division
feels a live-bird glut twice.

Sreeya Sewu is an integrated poultry company with three reported segments: animal feed, breeder and farm, and dressed chicken and frozen foods. In FY2025 the feed segment sold 2,598 IDR bn of external revenue, breeder and farm 1,482 IDR bn, and dressed chicken and frozen foods 1,361 IDR bn [S3]. Those figures add to more than consolidated sales because 1,291 IDR bn of inter-segment sales were eliminated on consolidation [S3] — the feed mills sell to the group's own farms and the farms sell birds to the processing plants.

**Feed.** Feed is the largest external business and the anchor of the group. Installed capacity was held at 750,000 MT tonnes a year and output was 464,926 MT tonnes in FY2025 [S5], leaving substantial idle capacity. The company makes broiler, layer, breeder, duck and quail feed and concentrates [S5]. The product is sold through distributors and directly to farms; the customer is a price-taking farmer whose willingness to pay is set by the live-bird market, not by the feed mill's cost.

**Breeder and farm.** The segment produces day-old chicks and live birds, with output of 103,275,912 head head in FY2025 [S5]. This is where the current industry configuration is most painful. The trade press in November 2026 put the farm-gate live-bird price at Rp17,000/kg per kilogramme against an independent producer's cost of production of Rp22,500/kg [S6]. A farmer selling below cost does not keep buying chicks at the old price, so a breeder's realisations fall faster than its volumes. The segment's external revenue fell year on year in FY2025 [S3], which is consistent with that mechanism already operating.

**Dressed chicken and frozen foods.** This is the value-added leg: slaughter, chill, cut and freeze, plus processed products. Capacity after the East Java processing investment is 76,466 MT tonnes a year against output of 45,769 MT tonnes [S5]. The strategic logic is sound — moving from a commodity bird into a branded, chilled and frozen product improves the price per kilogramme and reduces exposure to the live-bird cycle. The financial logic is harder: a segment running at roughly 50.0% per cent utilisation carries a fixed-cost base it cannot yet cover, and the capital spent to build the capacity was funded with debt that now costs more than the segment earns.

**Strategy.** Three strands are visible in the filings. The first is downstream integration, of which the East Java processing plant is the clearest expression [S5]. The second is raw-material security: raw materials are 60.0% per cent or more of production cost by the annual report's own framing [S5], and corn is the largest single input in a broiler ration, so procurement is a core activity rather than a support function. What the filings do not show is a company-specific supply concession. The government does run a feed-corn supply programme through the food agency, but the 242 000 MT thousand tonnes [S7] is the national allocation for every recipient in the programme — co-operatives and smallholders among them — and no filing we hold names Sreeya Sewu as a beneficiary. We therefore do not credit the company with preferential corn, and the bull case does not assume it. The third strand is cost discipline, which follows directly from the input mix: the only lever management controls without a price is conversion efficiency and overhead.

**Footprint and group.** The company is listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by PT Great Giant Pineapple, which held 90.8% per cent at the last annual report [S5]. The remaining 9.2% per cent is public [S5]. That ownership structure is the most important fact about the equity as a tradeable instrument, and we return to it in the governance section.

The group's controlling shareholder has its origins in pineapple plantation and processing. That
history matters more than it looks: a plantation parent brings a commodity-cyclical, capital-intensive
habit of mind to a business that is also commodity-cyclical and capital-intensive. Integrated poultry
in this market has historically been built by groups that control the feed mill, because the mill is
where the scale economics live and because owning the mill gives the group a captive outlet for its
own corn and by-products.

**Demand.** Poultry is the cheapest animal protein available to an Indonesian household and the category has grown with the population and with formal employment for a generation. The demand driver is not discretionary income; it is the price of protein relative to rice and tempeh. That makes volumes relatively stable and prices relatively volatile, which is exactly the configuration that punishes a producer with a fixed cost base and no pricing power [S5].

**The cost side is the industry.** A broiler ration is mostly corn and soybean meal, with a protein and energy premix. Corn is domestic and seasonal; soybean meal is imported and dollar-denominated. The November trade press put corn at Rp7,800/kg per kilogramme and imported soybean meal at Rp10,000/kg, with compound feed selling franco farm at about Rp10,000/kg [S6]. Those figures define the economics of the sector: the mill buys corn and meal on a market, blends them, and sells a product whose price the farmer will only pay if the bird is profitable. When corn rises, the mill's margin compresses until the feed price is reset, and the reset takes a quarter or two because customers resist and contracts lag.

Our house agricultural deck carries corn at US$215/t for the year and US$215/t next, against a spot of US$175/t, and soybean meal at US$411/t and US$411/t against a spot of US$361/t. Read plainly, the deck says the cost base stays high through the forecast year and does not ease materially after that. For a company whose FY2025 gross margin was 9.1% [S3], that is the whole story.

**Policy.** Two policy channels matter. The first is corn supply. The government runs a feed-corn supply programme through the food agency which sells corn at a set reference price to co-operatives, who pass it to smallholder farmers; the allocation for the programme is 242 000 MT thousand tonnes for the year across all recipients, and the agency's own reporting puts delivery to smallholders at a small fraction of that target [S7]. The mechanism exists to hold the farm-gate feed cost down, not to hand a margin to a listed mill, and nothing in that reporting names Sreeya Sewu. We treat the programme as a cap on how far the domestic corn price can run, not as a company cost advantage. The channel matters in the other direction: cheap corn to registered smallholders keeps them in business as buyers of compound feed, which supports the mill's volume rather than its unit margin. On the company's side, the annual report notes that corn reached around Rp7,000/kg per kilogramme in the fourth quarter of 2025 [S5] — a level that, if sustained, is above what the current feed price can absorb.

The second is the live-bird market. When the farm-gate price falls below the farmer's cost of production, as it did in November 2026 with the bird at Rp17,000/kg against production cost of Rp22,500/kg [S6], the policy response is usually culling or restrictions on chick placement. Both reduce feed and DOC volumes. The industry's problem is therefore self-correcting only through a volume contraction that hits exactly the companies carrying the most fixed capacity.

**Competitive landscape.** Sreeya Sewu is a challenger, not a leader. The integrated poultry sector is dominated by far larger players with national feed networks, their own grandparent stock and distribution that reaches down to the sub-district. Sreeya Sewu's feed capacity of 750,000 MT tonnes and dressed capacity of 76,466 MT tonnes place it well below the scale of the largest integrators. Scale matters here for two reasons: it sets the buying price for corn and meal, and it sets the utilisation of fixed assets. A sub-scale mill pays more for its raw material and spreads its overhead over fewer tonnes — a double disadvantage that shows up exactly where it did, in the gross margin [S5].

The scale gap is not an assertion. CPIN sold 60.2 IDR tn in the first nine months of 2026 and earned an operating margin of 11.3%; JPFA, the second of the pair, earned 3.2 IDR tn of net profit over the same period [S9]. Sreeya Sewu, on a fraction of that revenue, lost 59.2 IDR bn [S4]. The house covers CPIN and JPFA as buys and AYAM and WMPP as sells, which is the point: the sector contains winners and losers in the same nine months, so "the cycle" cannot be the whole explanation for a loss at this scale. Part of SIPD's problem is segment mix and part is scale, and both are company-specific — which is why we cut the weight on the recovery case rather than raise it.

**Asset value.** One cross-check does not depend on earnings, and it decides between our two methods. Replacing the feed mills, hatcheries and processing plants would cost of the order of the net property, plant and equipment on the balance sheet, 1,099.0 [S3]. If the equity can be bought for less than the net debt plus a fraction of that replacement value, the asset gets bought rather than built — that is what underpins the book leg. The operating business as run does not earn a return that justifies the asset, which is what the DCF says. Both are true at once: the assets are worth roughly book, and the earnings are not worth the assets.

The washout case is the same test with a recovered margin. The company's own best recent year earned a gross margin of 9.4% and an EBIT margin of 1.8% [S3], and our bull case takes the gross margin back to exactly that level with the deck's terminal inputs — no better. At today's price the market is already paying 9.0x of last year's EBITDA and 0.9x of book for a business whose best recent operating margin was 1.8%, so the shares discount a recovery better than any year in the record. That is the arithmetic the price has to justify, and why the asset value supports a target far below the market rather than above it.

The advantage the company does have is integration from feed through breeder to processing, which gives it an internal outlet for feed in a weak market and a route to a branded product. The advantage is real but defensive: it protects the franchise, it does not earn a premium return [S5].

**Five forces.** Supplier power is high and rising — corn is seasonal and policy-mediated, soybean meal is imported and priced in dollars, and neither can be substituted at short notice. Buyer power is high — the farmer negotiates on price and will switch mill for a few rupiah per kilogramme, and the modern-retail buyer of dressed chicken is a concentrated counterparty. New entry is constrained by capital and by the licensing of feed mills and processing plants, but not constrained enough to protect incumbents' returns. Substitutes at the consumer level are eggs, fish and frozen imports. Rivalry is severe and cyclical, made worse by the fact that the largest players can absorb losses that would sink a smaller one. On the evidence of the last three years of returns, the industry structure supports volume and cash flow but not economic profit for anyone below the top of the cost curve [S5][S6].

**External influences.** Two are live. The rupiah matters twice: soybean meal is imported and debt is partly floating-rate. Interest rates matter directly, because the company carries debt of 982 IDR bn against equity of 1,179 IDR bn [S4].

Indonesian poultry has a long history of boom and bust driven by chick placement. When prices are good
everyone places more chicks, the birds arrive at market together, the price collapses, farmers stop
placing, supply tightens, and the cycle restarts. Feed millers see the amplitude at one remove and
processors at two removes, which is why the integrated model smooths earnings without eliminating the
cycle. Government intervention in the corn market has the same character: it supports the farmer in a
deficit year and caps the mill in a surplus year.

**Revenue.** Net sales were 5,441.5 in FY2025 against 5,360.8 in FY2024 [S3] — a year of essentially flat top line. Behind the flat total the three legs diverged: the dressed-chicken segment's gross profit fell to 151 IDR bn from 188 IDR bn, while feed rose to 240 IDR bn from 227 IDR bn [S3]. The value-added leg is the one that lost money, not the commodity mill, and that matters for how the recovery has to arrive. The first nine months of 2026 show 4,301 IDR bn [S4], growth on a like-for-like basis driven by price rather than volume: the feed price rose with the corn price, so the top line grew while the margin fell. We forecast 5,871.4 for the year, then 6,194.4 and 6,504.1 as utilisation improves modestly and the deck's raw-material prices feed through into the selling price.

**The depreciation restatement.** This is the most important adjustment in the model and the reader should understand it before reading any multiple. Sreeya Sewu, like most IDX issuers, reports its cash-flow statement on the direct method. The data pack derives cash flow from the profit statement and, in doing so, picks up a depreciation figure that is a small fraction of the true charge. The audited segment note gives total depreciation and amortisation of 98.2 IDR bn for FY2025 and 93.8 IDR bn for FY2024, covering property, plant and equipment, right-of-use assets and intangibles [S3]. We use those. EBITDA is rebuilt from them at 183.5 and 157.7.

Everything downstream changes. The EV/EBITDA multiple at the market price is 9.0x on the restated base, not the multiple a screen shows. The DCF's terminal value is built off a cash flow that adds back the real charge rather than the pack's. And the reported D&A series is itself informative: capex of 182.3 and 270.2 ran above the charge of 98.2 and 93.8 in both years [S3], so the asset base is still growing. A growing asset base against a thin operating margin is how a company outgrows its own returns, and that is the pattern here rather than a shrinking depreciation cushion.

**Margins and costs.** FY2025 gross margin was 9.1% on cost of sales of 4,945.5 [S3]. Raw materials used were 4,429 IDR bn, and management's own framing puts raw material at 60.0% per cent or more of production cost [S5] — the two statements are consistent once you notice that cost of sales includes the trading and processing legs as well as the mill. Operating expense was 410.7, leaving EBIT of 85.3 and an EBIT margin of 1.6%. That is the number to hold in mind: a business with 5,441.5 of sales converts to an EBIT margin of 1.6% in a good year.

Our forecast has the gross margin at 7.4% for the current year, recovering to 7.9% and 8.4%. The bridge has two parts and they point in opposite directions, so the reader should see both. The first is input cost: corn and soybean meal enter cost of sales through two linked shares of the cost base, each with a partial pass-through, and the deck series beyond the last sourced point escalates at long-run inflation. The shares themselves are not taken from the deck's year-average percentage: they are calibrated on the witnessed domestic move, corn from Rp7,000/kg per kilogramme in the fourth quarter of 2025 to Rp7,800/kg in November 2026 [S5][S6], and on the imported meal price of Rp10,000/kg [S6], because the deck's year-average change overstates what a feed mill in this market actually paid. On its own that path would push the margin down in the forecast year and up thereafter as escalation slows. The second is mix: the dressed-chicken leg carried the highest gross margin of the three and its margin is what collapsed in FY2025, so the blended margin we forecast is lower than a pure input-cost model would give. We calibrated the pass-through so the model reproduces the witnessed nine-month 2026 margin from the FY2025 starting point — an evidence-fitted parameter, not a haircut [S3][S4] — and then applied a small downward drift of under a percentage point to carry the mix effect through the forecast. That drift is the one forecast assumption in this report that lowers the value; it is sourced to the segment note, and it is why our gross margin is below the pure cost model.

**Phasing and the fourth quarter.** The forecast looks lopsided, and we owe the reader an explanation rather than a defence. Nine-month EBIT was negative [S4], so the whole of the swing to a full-year EBIT of -30.0 has to come in the final quarter, and on an EBITDA of 72.7 most of the year's EBITDA sits there too. That is arithmetic, not optimism: when the first nine months lose money, any positive full year is back-loaded. The test is whether the implied fourth quarter is stronger than a normal seasonal quarter, and it is not. The fourth quarter of 2025 was the seasonal high because farmers restock before the holiday period; it also carried the bulk of that year's fair-value credit of 49.1 IDR bn, of which only 9.2 IDR bn had been booked by September [S3][S4]. Strip the credit and that quarter's operating result was still several times the nine-month quarterly run-rate. Our implied fourth quarter of 2026 comes in below that ex-credit level, not above it. Nor is the EBITDA concentration a depreciation artefact: nine-month depreciation of 81.1 IDR bn already ran close to the whole of the prior year's charge of 98.2 [S4][S3], so the fourth-quarter add-back is lighter than a normal quarter's share. A year carried by the final three months at a weaker operating result than last year's final three months is a weak year, and the rating does not depend on it.

**Cash flow and capital intensity.** The business consumes cash. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was -59.3 after capex of 182.3 [S3], because the working capital build absorbed the EBITDA. FY2026 is worse: -240.9 as inventory and receivables carry the higher corn price and the company funds a loss. The model turns free cash flow positive only in -7.6 after capex is cut back towards the depreciation charge. That is the assumption we would most like to be wrong about, because the company has a history of spending ahead of demand — the East Java plant is the proof [S5].

**Working capital and the balance sheet.** Non-cash working capital was 519.4, a normal intensity for a trader-processor that holds corn and settles with distributors on terms. The problem is leverage. At 30 September 2026 the company reported cash of 117 IDR bn and total debt on its own definition of 982 IDR bn, against equity of 1,179 IDR bn [S4]. Net debt is therefore close to the whole of book equity and the interest line has become the largest single call on operating profit: finance costs were 44.5 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 against EBIT that turned negative [S4]. Interest expense in FY2025 was 59.4 against interest income of 7.3, and the gap widens in our forecast as the debt taken on in 2026 is carried for a full year.

The year-end net debt our model produces is 800.6 against the 982 IDR bn of debt less 117 IDR bn of cash reported for September, and the reader should know why the two differ rather than discover it. Our forecast rolls only the borrowings that move with the financing line; the company's own definition includes lease liabilities and supplier financing, whose balance changes with the rupiah and with lease additions rather than with our cash-flow build. The valuation does not use the softer forecast figure: the DCF and the cross-checks deduct the September actual, because that is the last number a shareholder can verify. The cost of debt in the model is a single pre-tax rate of 9.4% used both in the cost of capital and in the interest line, which reproduces the charge the company actually booked on its opening debt [S4]. We do not run a lower rate for the P&L and a higher one for the WACC.
**Earnings quality.** The house screen produces four findings, one of them disqualifying for any value argument built on reported earnings [S3][S4].

*Cash conversion.* Net profit in FY2025 was 29.3, and free cash flow after capex was -59.3 [S3]. Earnings ran ahead of cash by the whole of the capex and working capital build. The accruals ratio is not the mechanism — the cash is genuinely spent on assets and inventory — but the conclusion is the same: the profit and loss account overstates what the business produced.

*Depreciation adequacy.* Capex of 182.3 in FY2025 and 270.2 in FY2024 against a depreciation charge of 98.2 and 93.8 means the company is still investing above its charge after a period of heavy expansion [S3]. An ageing asset base and a rising share of right-of-use depreciation is not a quality signal.

*Related parties.* Purchases from related parties were 16.1 IDR bn, a fraction of a per cent of cost of sales [S3]. Key management short-term compensation was 23.3 IDR bn [S3]. Neither is a red flag on its own; both are disclosed properly and the quantum is small.

*Fair-value credits on biological assets.* This is the finding that matters most for the valuation. The income statement carries a fair-value gain on biological assets of 49.1 IDR bn inside the FY2025 operating result and 9.2 IDR bn inside the nine-month 2026 result [S3][S4]. It is a gain recognised in the profit statement that reflects the directors' determinable fair value — a mark-to-model on live birds and hatching eggs priced off projected selling prices and feed costs [S4] — and it sits inside the EBITDA we use, because the segment note does not separate it out. Strip it from last year's restated EBITDA and the multiple we quote on reported EBITDA understates the true one by roughly a third; strip it from the current year and the EBITDA we forecast is smaller than it looks. We keep the reported figure in the model so that our EBITDA reconciles with the market's convention, and we name it here so no reader is surprised. A valuation that rests on a mark-to-model credit is leaning on the live-bird price [S6], and that is not a foundation we would build on.

*Inventory and provision risk.* The company carries live birds and feed inventory at fair value less cost to sell. In a falling live-bird market that valuation is a source of provision risk, and it is the line we watch after every reporting date. The November farm-gate price of Rp17,000/kg against cost of production of Rp22,500/kg [S6] is exactly the configuration that produces a writedown, and it is why the fair-value credit has already shrunk from the FY2025 level.

**IDX regime status.** The annual report states that the shares were not suspended or delisted during the year and that all listing requirements were met [S5]. There is no special-notation letter to discount. That statement is made against the rules in force during the year, and it does not contradict the float shortfall in the governance section: the higher public-shareholding minimum is being raised under a new rule with a phased implementation [S8], so a company can be compliant with what applied in FY2025 and still sit below the level that will apply. We report the shortfall because it is forward supply, not because it is a breach. The corporate-governance structure is conventional: a board of commissioners with an independent member, an audit committee, and an unqualified Big Four audit opinion (see the governance section).

**Why this method set.** Poultry feed is a volume business with a thin, cyclical margin, a fixed asset base and a leveraged balance sheet. The appropriate primary method is a discounted cash flow, because the value of the business is the cash it can distribute after the capex and working capital its volume requires — and because reported earnings are distorted by a depreciation charge the market does not see. We cross-check against EV/EBITDA, the multiple the sector trades on, which is robust to the distortion once EBITDA is rebuilt, and against price-to-book, the only method that says anything at all when earnings are negative. We do not use a P/E: after nine months of losses there is no trailing multiple, and a forward one would rest on a recovery our own model does not support.
**Cost of capital.**

The build is conventional for an Indonesian small cap. The risk-free rate is 7.4% on the long rupiah bond, the mature-market equity premium 4.2%, and the country risk premium 2.5%. We use an unlevered beta of 0.90 — the industry default, because the house has no regression for poultry feed and we will not invent one from a peer set of four. Levered at the market debt-to-equity ratio of 0.85 and a tax rate of 22.0%, that gives a levered beta of 1.50 and a cost of equity of 15.8%. The pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, the rate the company's floating facilities imply and the rate we also charge in the profit and loss account [S3][S4]. At the market weights the WACC is 12.0%, inside the house band for an Indonesian compounder of this kind.

The cost of equity is above that band, and we say so rather than bury it. It is not an illiquidity premium dressed as a discount rate. It is the arithmetic of leverage: an unlevered beta at the industry default, carried through a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.85 at a tax rate of 22.0%, produces a levered beta of 1.50, and multiplying a levered beta of that size by a mature premium plus a country premium gives 15.8% whatever we would prefer. To pull the cost of equity inside the band we would have to cut the unlevered beta to a level no feed miller in this market has ever earned — that would be a fabrication, not a judgement. The WACC stays inside the band because the company is financed roughly half by debt, and it is the WACC that discounts the cash flows. The instrument risk we cannot put in beta we charge once, explicitly, as the liquidity discount below.
**Primary method: DCF.**

Free cash flow to the firm is built from the restated EBITDA, taxed at the statutory rate, less capex and less the working capital the volume requires [S3][S4]. The enterprise value comes out at 405.5, with 82.7% of it in the terminal value — a high share, but not unusual for a business that only turns cash-positive late in the explicit period. Once the September net debt is deducted, the equity value is zero and the per-share value is Rp0.

We should be explicit about that zero, because a reader is entitled to ask whether it is a modelling artefact. It is not. The DCF's verdict is that the operating assets, discounted at a cost of capital consistent with the risk, are worth less than the debt against them: unfloored, the equity shortfall is larger than the discounted enterprise value itself. That is what a return on invested capital in the low single digits against a cost of capital of 12.0% produces when terminal growth is long-run inflation.

The floor matters for how the reader should use this method. The enterprise value of 405.5 is a fraction of the net property, plant and equipment on the last balance sheet, 1,099.0 [S3], and a still smaller fraction of book equity of 1,179 IDR bn plus net debt at September [S4]. The cash-flow model is not saying the mills, hatcheries and plants are worthless. It is saying that as operated, and after the working capital and capex their volume requires, they cannot service the capital that funded them. We use the DCF to test whether the asset can earn its cost of capital — it cannot — and we value the equity off book because book is what a buyer of the asset would start from.
**Cross-checks.**

The peer-median EV/EBITDA of 4.7 is applied to last year's restated EBITDA of 183.5 [S3], not to a trough year — the check should be run on the earnings the market can see, and using the forecast trough would flatter the method by shrinking its denominator. Even on that kinder base the implied enterprise value does not reach the September net debt, so the equity value is small and negative; the blend floors it at zero. That agreement is informative: two methods failing in the same direction, for the same reason, are not independent confirmations of a number but a joint statement that the capital structure is the dominant fact. For completeness, the house default for this cross-check would be the company's own history, whose mean EV/EBITDA is very high precisely because the pack's depreciation understatement inflates the denominator's mirror image elsewhere in the model; we override it to the peer median because an own-history multiple computed on a corrupted EBITDA history is not a cross-check at all.

Price-to-book gives Rp617 at a multiple of 1.0. That is where the target comes from. The house default for the book leg is the company's own trading history, and we override it to the peer median. The reader should see both, because the override is against the company and it is material: the company's own mean price-to-book is roughly twice the peer median, so the default would take this leg close to the current share price and the target would be substantially higher. We do not use it. The own history is a record of what the market paid in years when this business earned a return on equity it no longer produces, and importing that premium into a target that assumes the present losses continue would be double-counting a past the company has left. The peer median asks only what the market pays for a feed integrator's book today. Note what we are assuming either way: that the balance-sheet value of the feed mills, hatcheries and processing plants is recoverable, and that the company can be run for cash rather than for growth. If the losses continue, the book erodes and this leg falls with it.

Now the chain, in one place and in order. The weights are 50% DCF, 20% EV/EBITDA and 30% P/BV. Because the first two return exactly zero, the weighted blend is the book leg times its weight: Rp185. That blend is today's value; rolled forward at the cost of equity to the target date it is Rp214. Applied to our three scenarios with their probabilities it is Rp270 — and the lift from base to weighted is the bull case alone, because the bear case sits below the base and carries the larger weight. The probability weighting is why the weighted number is above the base number, and a reader who disagrees with the bull probability should read the target off the base. Finally the liquidity discount of 30% gives Rp189.

That discount is not a rounding device and it is not a second bite at the risk premium. It is the house charge for instruments a fund cannot exit, set from the traded-value bands in the constitution rather than from judgement, and charged exactly once: it applies to the equity value, not to the discount rate, which is why the cost of equity above is an unlevered-beta result and not an illiquidity premium in disguise. The arithmetic is blunt. The entire free float is 9.1% of a market capitalisation of 1,158,634,295,280.0, and the shares trade 51,259,258.1 a day [S0]. A fund selling a position of any size is the market. For the same reason this SELL is a view on value rather than an instruction we can execute: with no borrow available at this float, the rating speaks to an owner deciding whether to hold, not to a short seller.

**Reinvestment and owner earnings.** The valuation rests on the book leg, so the reader should see what the operating business actually hands back. In FY2025 the company reinvested more than its entire after-tax operating profit: capex of 182.3 plus the working capital build against after-tax EBIT on an EBIT of 85.3 [S3], which is why free cash flow to the firm was -59.3. The incremental return on that reinvestment is the number that decides whether growth is worth anything, and on the segment record it is not: the feed margin improved only fractionally on a larger capital base while the dressed-chicken leg earned less gross profit on more capacity [S3]. Owner earnings — EBITDA of 183.5 less the capex needed to hold the asset base, less cash interest of 59.4 and cash tax — come to roughly nothing in FY2025. That is the honest starting point, and it is why the DCF's fade assumption is not a horror story: there is no value-creating spread to fade from.
**Sensitivity.**

The grid is dominated by a boundary, and the boundary is the finding. For any WACC above the model's central case, or any growth below it, the DCF equity value is already zero and stays there, so the table shows no response along that edge — that is the floor, not a broken table. Only a materially lower cost of capital combined with materially higher terminal growth lifts the DCF above the debt, and neither is inside the range we consider reasonable for this balance sheet. The live axis is the book multiple: because the target is the book leg times its weight, the target moves almost proportionally with the peer multiple that prices it. That is what we mean when we say the shares are a leveraged claim on book value rather than on cash flow, and it is the axis a reader should stress, not the WACC.

We also tested the input path a reader is most likely to propose: the deck's spot instead of its year-average as the current-year cost. It is the right direction of risk and it improves the current-year margin by more than the base case assumes. We did not adopt it because the deck's spot is one day's print, while the company's own November corn price of Rp7,800/kg against Rp7,000/kg last year is the move a mill actually paid [S6][S5]. A sustained lower input price belongs in the bull case, which is where we put it, with the gross margin anchored on the FY2023 realised level.

**What the price implies.** At Rp630 the equity is capitalised at 0.9x of book and the enterprise at 9.0x of last year's restated EBITDA, 26.9x of the current year's and 17.3x of next year's. For contrast, our target implies an exit at close to the peer median on terminal-year EBITDA: the target does not ask a future buyer to pay today's multiple, which is the whole difference between buying an asset and buying a hope. To earn today's multiples the company would have to lift its EBIT margin far above anything in our record — the FY2025 margin was 1.6% and no year in the last five came close to the level the price requires. The reverse DCF does not produce a bracketing growth rate at all: the price sits above the entire plausible range of the model, so the implied growth is not a number we can honestly place. When a reverse DCF cannot bracket the price, the market is valuing something that is not in the cash flows — here, most plausibly, the controlling shareholder's option value or a control premium a minority holder cannot access.
**Downside risks, with likelihood and impact.**

*Raw-material spread (high likelihood, high impact).* Corn and soybean meal are the cost base, and the deck keeps both above last year's average into the forecast year [S6]. A further move of the kind seen between FY2025 and the current year would deepen the loss rather than merely compress the margin. This is the risk that has already materialised.

*Live-bird and DOC price (high likelihood, high impact).* The farm-gate price was Rp17,000/kg against production cost of Rp22,500/kg in November 2026 [S6]. Farmers operating below cost cut placements, which hits the breeder segment first and the feed segment next. The company's breeder revenue already fell in FY2025 [S3].

*Leverage and refinancing (medium likelihood, high impact).* Debt of 982 IDR bn against equity of 1,179 IDR bn [S4], with floating-rate bank facilities [S3], means a rate rise or a covenant renegotiation is a solvency question rather than an earnings question. The company pays no dividend and has no obvious equity story to raise against.

*Regulatory and policy (medium likelihood, medium impact).* The feed-corn supply programme is a national allocation of 242 000 MT thousand tonnes for all recipients, delivered through co-operatives to smallholders rather than to listed mills [S7]; we credit the company with no share of it. The policy risk runs through the price: if the programme's delivery stays small, the domestic corn price is set by the open market and by the import quota for soybean meal, and a change to either moves the cost base without warning.

*Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).* Soybean meal is imported and priced in dollars; the house macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD next year. A weaker rupiah raises the meal cost directly.

*Operational (low likelihood, medium impact).* Disease, a plant outage or a food-safety recall in the dressed-chicken business would hit the segment that already runs at roughly 50.0% per cent utilisation [S5].

*Governance (medium likelihood, medium impact).* A controlling shareholder at 90.8% per cent [S5] determines related-party terms, capital actions and the timing of any float increase. The minority has no ability to force a value-realising event.

*Competitive position (high likelihood, high impact).* The loss is company-specific, not sector-wide: over the same nine months in which Sreeya Sewu lost 59.2 IDR bn [S4], CPIN earned 5.2 IDR tn of net profit on an operating margin of 11.3% and JPFA 3.2 IDR tn, both up on the year [S9]. Buyers are switching to mills that can price better, and a challenger with sub-scale feed capacity of 750,000 MT tonnes against the leaders' national networks loses volume first when farmers retrench [S5]. This is the risk that most directly caps the bull case.

*Liquidity (high likelihood, high impact for a holder).* The float is the exit problem. Public shareholders hold 9.2% per cent against an exchange minimum of 15.0% per cent [S5][S8], and the phased compliance path is set by the exchange rather than by the company's timetable. A sell-down to meet the threshold is supply into a book that trades tens of millions of rupiah a day.
**Scenarios.**

We use three scenarios with probabilities of 50% base, 35% bear and 15% bull, and the shocks are exact mirrors: revenue growth, gross margin and working capital intensity move by the same amount in opposite directions in bear and bull. The bear case is a deeper and longer raw-material squeeze with the margin staying depressed and working capital absorbing more cash, plus the supply from any float-driven selldown. The bull case is a normalisation of corn and meal towards the deck's later years, the cull that follows a year of farm-gate losses cutting placements and restoring live-bird and DOC prices, and utilisation improving in dressed chicken. Its gross margin lands at 9.4% — the best year in the record, not an invented upside — which is the test a bull case should have to pass.

The base probability is half rather than evenly split, and the bull is a sixth rather than a third, for one reason: the sector recovery is already visible at the scaled players [S9], so a cyclical rebound alone does not reach a sub-scale integrator with negative operating profit. The bull needs a company-specific repair of utilisation and mix on top of the cycle, which is the harder half of the story. We would rather be honest about that than flatter the case we are arguing against.

The presentation produces an uncomfortable result that we will not hide: the bear and base targets are the same, Rp214 and Rp214. The reason is structural. In both scenarios the earnings-based methods return no equity value, and the P/BV leg is anchored on today's book, which the scenario shocks do not touch directly. The scenarios therefore differ in the path, not the endpoint: in the bear case the path runs through losses that erode book and eventually take the target down with it, while in the base case book is preserved. A reader should treat the bear case as understating the downside, and the bull case, at Rp582, as the value the company would be worth if the margin recovered to the level of its own best year and the market paid a peer multiple for it.

**The exit we do not model separately.** A tender offer or squeeze-out is a real outcome at this ownership and this float, and the engine's three scenarios do not carry it as a fourth line. We fold it into the bull case: a control event is the one route by which a minority holder is paid above our target, which is a reason the bull weight is not lower, not a reason to raise the target. Our bargaining position is weak — the float is small enough to be bought for a sum immaterial against the parent's balance sheet, and the shares trade 51,259,258.1 a day [S0]. The block placement is its mirror and sits inside the bear case as supply.

**Signposts that change the view.** A sustained fall in the domestic corn price towards the deck's spot, with the feed price held, would lift the gross margin above our forecast. A farm-gate live-bird price above the producer cost of production would restore breeder volumes and pricing. A capital action that reduces debt — an asset sale, a rights issue at a sensible price, or a refinancing at a lower spread — would change the capital-structure arithmetic behind the DCF's zero. On the other side, a profit warning for FY2026, a covenant breach, or a deeply discounted placement to meet the float requirement would confirm the bear path.

**Ownership and control.** PT Great Giant Pineapple held 90.8% per cent of the shares at the last annual report, with 9.2% per cent held by the public [S5]. Control is absolute. There is no second blockholder, no activist route and no realistic prospect of a contested vote. For a minority investor the relevant question is not who runs the company but what the controller chooses to do with it, and the answer in the last two years has been to retain earnings and fund expansion [S5].

**The free float.** The exchange minimum for public shareholding is now 15.0% per cent, phased for companies already listed [S8], against a public holding of 9.2% per cent [S5]. The company is therefore below the threshold, and the phased timetable is the exchange's, not ours; we do not put a date on it because we have not sourced one. This is an operating fact with a valuation consequence, not a footnote: compliance requires the controller to sell, or the company to issue, a block equal to several percentage points of the shares outstanding into a market that trades a rounding error of the market capitalisation each day. The most likely mechanisms are a placement to an institutional investor at a discount or a secondary sell-down by the parent; both weigh on the mark, and the first would also raise questions about the pricing of any discounted issue to a related party.

**The exit route, and the two that do not exist.** With the free float where it is, there are only two ways value gets realised for a minority holder, and neither is on the company's agenda. The first is a tender offer: at a public holding of 9.2% per cent the free float is a small sum against the parent's balance sheet, so a take-private or a squeeze-out at a modest premium is cheap for the controller and devastating for anyone who bought higher. The second is a recovery in the operating margin, which is the bull case [S5][S8]. What does not exist is the third route most minority investors rely on: for a name this illiquid a short is not realistically available to us — we could identify no borrow, and the daily traded value is small enough that a fund's own exit would move the price [S8]. We are explicit about that because it is the difference between a target and a trade.

**Related parties.** Purchases from related parties were 16.1 IDR bn in FY2025, a fraction of a per cent of cost of sales [S3], and key management short-term benefits were 23.3 IDR bn [S3]. The disclosure is adequate and the quantum is not a value leak. We found no related-party sales of consequence and no guarantees to the controlling group's other ventures in the notes we reviewed.

**Pledged shares.** We searched the annual report and the interim filing for share pledges and found no disclosure of a pledge over the controlling stake [S5][S4]. That is not a clean bill of health — the absence of disclosure is normal until a pledge is enforced — but there is no evidence of margin-call supply overhanging the shares.

**Auditor and opinion.** The FY2025 statements were audited by KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan — the firm formerly known as Tanudiredja, Wibisana, Rintis & Rekan, which is PwC's Indonesian member firm — with Andry Danil Atmadja as signing partner [S5]. The report dated 27 March 2026 gives an unqualified opinion that the statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position and performance [S5]. This is a Big Four engagement, not a second-tier one, and the reader should not read the valuation's severity as a comment on audit quality. If anything the opposite: the audited notes are what let us find the real depreciation charge and the fair-value credit, and the market's data providers, not the auditor, are the ones who missed them.

**Board.** The board of commissioners comprises Antonius Joenoes Supit as President Commissioner concurrently serving as an independent commissioner, Stephanie Verawaty Gondokusumo as commissioner, and Theo Lekatompessy as independent commissioner [S5]. The combination of the chair and an independent seat in one person is common in Indonesian family-controlled companies and weakens the board as a check on the controller. There is an audit committee, and the annual report documents its work [S5].

**Dividend record.** The annual general meeting for FY2024 resolved not to distribute a cash dividend, allocated a small amount to the statutory reserve, and retained the remainder as working capital [S5]. That is consistent with the model's zero payout and with a company funding a capital programme and a working-capital cycle from retained earnings. It also means there is no income floor under the shares: the holder is paid nothing while waiting for the cycle to turn.

**ESG exposures.** The material issues are specific and mostly operational. On the environmental side, feed milling and processing are energy-intensive, and the company's exposure to corn links it to land use and to the sustainability of its smallholder supply base; the annual report sets out the sustainability framework and reports under the financial-services sustainability regulation [S5]. On the social side, food safety and halal assurance are the licence to operate: the company holds halal certification and good-manufacturing-practice certification for feed and slaughter [S5]. Animal welfare and antibiotic use in the breeder and farm segment are the issues most likely to attract scrutiny from export customers and modern-retail buyers. Governance is the weakest of the three pillars — a dominant controller, a combined chair and independent seat, and a float that does not yet meet the exchange minimum.
**Dated catalysts.**

blocks.text: **What we monitor between updates.** The weekly live-bird and DOC prices, because they set the farmer's willingness to pay for feed and the breeder segment's realisation [S6]. The domestic corn basis and the imported soybean-meal price, because together they set the cost line [S6]. The dressed-chicken utilisation rate, because half-capacity operation is where the segment's losses come from [S5]. Quarterly net debt and interest cover, because leverage is the transmission channel from a margin shock to an equity event [S4]. And the share register, because any movement in the public float towards the minimum is supply over the shares.

**What would make us wrong.** A structural, not cyclical, improvement in the feed margin — a sustained corn basis below the deck, a feed price reset that sticks, and a dressed-chicken segment approaching full utilisation — would raise the DCF above the debt and make the equity worth something in its own right. The evidence we would need is consecutive quarters of positive EBIT with a gross margin above the FY2025 level, and a reduction in net debt [S3]. Until that evidence exists, the equity is a claim on book value, and book value earns nothing.

bear.narrative: The chicken trough lasts. Live birds are already selling at the farm gate for IDR 17,000 to 18,000 a kilogram against a cost of production of IDR 22,500 to 23,000 (S6, F31, F32), so independent producers are losing money and demand for the DOC and feed SIPD sells them shrinks; corn at IDR 7,800 to 8,000 and imported soybean meal at IDR 10,000 keep the input bill high (S6, F33, F34) while the deck's forward curves stay above the 2025 level (S0). Working capital absorbs more of each rupiah as supplier terms tighten, and the free-float sale adds supply. Three shocks, each the mirror of the bull: growth three points lower, gross margin two points lower, working capital two points of revenue heavier.

bull.narrative: The cull works. Smallholders exit after a year of losses (S6), placements are cut and live bird and DOC prices recover into 2027, which pulls through both the breeder and farm segment and the dressed chicken line; feed volume returns toward the 750,000 MT of installed capacity from 464,926 MT (S5, F21, F22) and the East Java frozen-food plant, at about 50 per cent utilisation, absorbs its fixed cost (S5, F24, F26). The national SPHP feed-corn programme - 242 thousand tonnes for all recipients in 2026, sold below market through co-operatives to registered smallholders (S7, F37) - is a benefit to the sector, not an allocation to SIPD: it keeps the domestic corn price from spiking and keeps smallholders buying compound feed. No filing we hold names SIPD as a recipient, and the bull case does not assume one. The probability is 15 per cent rather than an even third because the sector recovery is already visible at the scaled players: CPIN grew nine-month 2026 net profit 53.82 per cent on an 11.33 per cent operating margin and JPFA 34 per cent on 9.50 per cent (S9, F43-F46), so a cyclical rebound does not by itself reach SIPD - the bull needs a company-specific repair of utilisation and mix, which is the harder half. Growth three points higher, gross margin two points higher and working capital two points of revenue lighter, exactly mirroring the bear.
